definition: Deregulation means the reduction or removal of government rules and restrictions controlling an industry or activity.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word deregulation. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know deregulation should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: After the deregulation of the telephone industry, dozens of new companies rushed in to compete for customers.
Relaxation is weaker than deregulation: relaxing the rules only eases a few requirements, while deregulation removes whole sections of the rulebook.
Dismantling is stronger than deregulation: deregulation trims or removes many rules, while dismantling the regulatory system tears the entire structure down.

Decontrol is the removal of one specific official control — most often a price cap or a quota — lifted one control at a time. Deregulation is broader: it strips away whole sections of the rulebook that governs an industry. Decontrol takes off a single control; deregulation shrinks the regime of rules itself.

Liberalization is the loosening of rules so markets can operate more freely, and it names a policy direction more than a single act — a market can be liberalized gradually over a decade. Deregulation is the concrete removal of the government rules themselves. Liberalization is where policy is heading; deregulation is the rulebook actually shrinking.

Deregulation means the reduction or removal of government rules and restrictions controlling an industry or activity.
For forty years, federal rules dictated which routes long-haul trucking companies could drive and what they could charge.
When Congress swept most of those rules away, the industry entered a period of rapid deregulation.
New carriers flooded the market, shipping rates fell, and established companies suddenly had to compete on price and service.
Economists still debate whether the change helped workers, but no one disputes how thoroughly the old rulebook was dismantled.
Removing the government rules that had controlled an entire industry is precisely what deregulation names.
economic and political register
Deregulation almost always describes a policy applied to a whole industry or market, such as airlines, energy, banking, or trucking, rather than to one person.
Its natural opposite is regulation, the building up of government rules, so the two words often appear together in debates about how free a market should be.

Until 1982, running an intercity bus line in the United States meant living inside a thick federal rulebook.
A company needed government permission for every route it drove, every fare it charged, and every city it added or dropped.
Applications could take years.
Then Congress passed a sweeping deregulation of the industry.
Route approvals, fare filings, and entry permits disappeared from the rulebook together.
New carriers flooded in within months.
Fares fell on busy corridors, and discount lines appeared.
Not every change was welcome -- some small towns lost service entirely, since no rule now required anyone to drive there -- but the industry had been remade by subtraction.
